lessons.title: Packages on Red Hat family systems: rpm and dnf
lessons.goal:
Learn how to ask which package owns a file, inspect a package, and install and remove software with `dnf`.

Why it matters: installing from a package manager gives you dependency resolution, verification and clean removal. Copying files by hand gives you none of that.

setup.note: Steps with sudo change the system (they install and remove one small package). Use a throwaway machine.

steps.title: rpm: the low-level tool
steps.text: An **rpm** file is an archive of files plus metadata (name, version, dependencies, scripts). `rpm` installs and queries individual files, and it keeps a database of what is installed.

run.output:
Name        : coreutils
Version     : 8.32
Architecture: aarch64
License     : GPLv3+
Summary     : A set of basic GNU tools commonly used in shell scripts

steps.title: What is inside a package
steps.text: `rpm -ql` lists the files a package installed. `rpm -qR` lists what it requires.

steps.title: Verify that files are unchanged
steps.text: `rpm -V` compares the installed files with the database (size, checksum, mode, owner). No output means everything matches. A letter in the output marks a difference.

run.cmd: sudo sh -c 'echo x >> /usr/bin/tree'; rpm -V tree | cut -c1-12; sudo dnf -q -y reinstall tree 2>&1 | tail -n 1; rpm -V tree; echo "exit code: $?"

steps.after: `S.5....T.` means: Size, md5/sha digest and mtime changed. After the reinstall the file is original again.

steps.title: dnf: the high-level tool
steps.text: `dnf` reads **repositories** (online catalogs of packages), solves dependencies, downloads and calls rpm. `dnf repolist` lists the enabled repositories. The option `-C` means "use the cached metadata", which is much faster than refreshing it every time.

run.output:
Name         : dos2unix
Version      : 7.4.2
Repository   : ol9_baseos_latest
Summary      : Text file format converters
Name         : dos2unix
Version      : 7.4.2
Repository   : ol9_baseos_latest
Summary      : Text file format converters

steps.title: Install and remove
steps.text: `dnf install` brings in the package and everything it needs. `dnf remove` takes out the package. `rpm -q` shows whether it is installed.

run.cmd: sudo dnf -q -y install dos2unix 2>&1 | tail -n 2; rpm -q dos2unix
sudo dnf -q -y remove dos2unix 2>&1 | tail -n 1; rpm -q dos2unix

steps.title: Which package provides a file?
steps.text: When a command is missing, find out which package contains it. `dnf provides` searches the repositories, including packages that are not installed.

run.output:
dos2unix-7.4.2-4.el9.aarch64 : Text file format converters
Repo        : ol9_baseos_latest

steps.under: Installed packages are recorded in the rpm database under `/var/lib/rpm`. The dependency solver (libsolv) loads the metadata of all enabled repositories and finds a set of packages that satisfies every requirement without conflicts. That is why you should not delete package files by hand: the database would still list them.

quiz.q: Which command shows the package that owns `/usr/bin/ls`?
What does `rpm -V PKG` print when nothing changed?
quiz.explain: Silence means the installed files match the database.

quiz.q: What does dnf do that plain rpm does not?
quiz.explain: dnf downloads and installs what is needed.

quiz.q: A command is not found. How do you find the package that provides it?

check.scenario: You suspect someone replaced /usr/bin/ssh with a trojan. How do you check on an RPM system, and what is the limit of that check?
check.answer: `rpm -Vf /usr/bin/ssh` (or `rpm -Va` for everything) compares the file with the database; changed size or digest shows up. The limit: an attacker with root can also change the database or the `rpm` binary. For a trusted check boot from known-good media or compare against the vendor package (`rpm -K`, `dnf reinstall` and compare).

lessons.title: Packages on Debian family systems: dpkg and apt
lessons.goal:
Learn the Debian equivalents of rpm and dnf and how to translate between the two worlds.

Why it matters: many servers run Ubuntu or Debian. The concepts are identical, only the commands differ.

setup.note: This lesson uses an Ubuntu container so you can see the Debian tools. If you have an Ubuntu or Debian machine, skip the first line and run the commands there without `sudo docker exec ubu`.
commands: sudo docker rm -f ubu >/dev/null 2>&1; sudo docker run -d --name ubu ubuntu:24.04 sleep 3600 >/dev/null

steps.title: dpkg: the low-level tool
steps.text: `.deb` packages are installed and queried by `dpkg`. `dpkg -S FILE` finds the owner of a file (like `rpm -qf`), `dpkg -L PKG` lists files (like `rpm -ql`).

run.output: dpkg-query: no path found matching pattern /bin/ls

run.cmd: sudo docker exec ubu dpkg -l bash | tail -n 1 | awk '{print $1, $2, $3}'
sudo docker exec ubu dpkg -L coreutils | head -n 3

steps.title: apt: repositories and dependencies
steps.text: `apt` is the high-level tool. Repositories are listed in `/etc/apt/sources.list.d/`. `apt-get update` downloads the package lists. Nothing is installed by it.

run.cmd: sudo docker exec ubu sh -c 'grep -E "^(Types|URIs|Suites)" /etc/apt/sources.list.d/ubuntu.sources | head -n 3'
run.output:
Types: deb
URIs: http://ports.ubuntu.com/ubuntu-ports/
Suites: noble noble-updates noble-backports

run.cmd: sudo docker exec ubu sh -c 'apt-get update -qq 2>&1 | tail -n 2; echo "update exit: $?"'

steps.title: Install, inspect, remove
steps.text: `apt-get install` resolves and installs dependencies. `apt-cache depends` shows what a package needs.

run.cmd: sudo docker exec ubu sh -c 'apt-get install -y -qq tree > /dev/null 2>&1; dpkg -l tree | tail -n 1 | awk "{print \$1, \$2}"'
sudo docker exec ubu apt-cache depends tree | head -n 3
sudo docker exec ubu sh -c 'apt-get remove -y -qq tree > /dev/null 2>&1; dpkg -l tree | tail -n 1 | awk "{print \$1, \$2}"'
run.output: dpkg-query: no packages found matching tree

steps.after: After `remove` the state is `rc`: the package is gone but its configuration files remain. `purge` would delete them too.

steps.title: The translation table
steps.text:
The concepts map one to one.

- Owner of a file: `rpm -qf FILE` / `dpkg -S FILE`
- Files of a package: `rpm -ql PKG` / `dpkg -L PKG`
- Installed list: `rpm -qa` / `dpkg -l`
- Refresh metadata: `dnf makecache` / `apt-get update`
- Install: `dnf install PKG` / `apt-get install PKG`
- Remove: `dnf remove PKG` / `apt-get remove PKG`
- Search: `dnf search WORD` / `apt-cache search WORD`
- Upgrade all: `dnf upgrade` / `apt-get upgrade`

run.cmd: sudo docker exec ubu sh -c 'apt-cache search "directory listing" | head -n 2 | cut -c1-70'
run.output:
libfile-listing-perl - module to parse directory listings
httpdirfs - filesystem client for HTTP directory listings

steps.under: Both systems keep a **database of installed files and versions** (`/var/lib/dpkg/status` and `/var/lib/rpm`) and a **dependency solver** over repository metadata. Package scripts (preinst, postinst) run as root, which is why you only add repositories you trust.

quiz.q: Which command finds the package that owns /bin/ls on Debian?

options: Downloads the package lists from the repositories

quiz.q: Which is the Debian counterpart of `dnf provides`?
quiz.explain: `apt-file search` (package apt-file) searches files in all repository packages.

check.scenario: An Ubuntu server shows `E: Unable to locate package foo`. List the likely causes.
check.answer:
1. You did not run `apt-get update`, so the package lists are empty or stale.
2. The package is in a repository that is not enabled (for example `universe`).
3. The name is wrong or differs by release.
4. No network or proxy to the mirror.

lessons.title: Building from source with make
lessons.goal:
Learn what happens in `./configure && make && make install`, how `make` decides what to rebuild, and why a source install is invisible to the package manager.

Why it matters: sometimes no package exists. You should know how to build safely, where the files go, and how to avoid a mess.

setup.note: Steps with sudo change the system (they install and remove one small package). Use a throwaway machine.

steps.title: A tiny project: the source
steps.text: `hello.c` is a program with one job. Save it as `hello.c`.

steps.title: The Makefile
steps.text: A **Makefile** lists **targets**, their **prerequisites** and the command to build each (the recipe). A recipe line must start with a TAB, not spaces. `make` rebuilds a target when a prerequisite is newer than it.

code.src:
PREFIX ?= /usr/local
CFLAGS ?= -O2 -Wall

hello: hello.o
	$(CC) -o $@ $<

hello.o: hello.c
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -c -o $@ $<

install: hello
	install -D -m 755 hello $(DESTDIR)$(PREFIX)/bin/hello

clean:
	rm -f hello hello.o

steps.title: Build
steps.text: `make` builds the first target, `hello`. It sees that `hello` needs `hello.o`, and `hello.o` needs `hello.c`, so it compiles first and links second.

run.output:
cc -O2 -Wall -c -o hello.o hello.c
cc -o hello hello.o

steps.title: make rebuilds only what changed
steps.text: A second `make` does nothing. After you change the source, only the affected steps run. `make -n` shows what it would do without doing it.

run.output:
cc -O2 -Wall -c -o hello.o hello.c
cc -o hello hello.o

cc -O2 -Wall -c -o hello.o hello.c
cc -o hello hello.o

steps.title: Install into a prefix, not the system
steps.text: `PREFIX` says where the program goes. `DESTDIR` is a staging root that packagers use. Installing under your own directory needs no root and is easy to remove.

steps.title: The package manager does not know about it
steps.text: Files you installed by hand are not in the rpm database. `rpm -qf` cannot find an owner, so updates and removal are your job.

run.output: file /tmp/lab/stage/usr/local/bin/hello is not owned by any package
hello: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, ARM aarch64

steps.under: `make` compares **modification times** of files. If the clock is wrong or files are copied with wrong times, builds go stale. The classic `./configure` script (autotools) checks your system and writes a Makefile; then `make` builds and `make install` copies the files. Prefer a package (`rpmbuild` or `checkinstall`) or a prefix such as `/opt/NAME` so uninstall is simple.

steps.title: The autotools recipe
steps.text: Most open-source tarballs use this sequence. The commands are shown here only; they need a project to build.

run.cmd: tar xf project-1.0.tar.gz && cd project-1.0 && ./configure --prefix=/opt/project && make -j"$(nproc)" && sudo make install
run.reason: needs a real source tarball; the Makefile steps above show the same stages

options: When a prerequisite is newer than the target
A staging root in front of the install paths
quiz.explain: Packagers install into a staging tree and then archive it.

quiz.q: Why is `make install` into /usr/local a maintenance problem?
options: The package manager cannot track or remove the files

quiz.q: What character must start a Makefile recipe line?
quiz.explain: Recipes are indented with a TAB.

check.scenario: You must install a newer tool than your distribution offers, on 20 servers, and be able to remove it cleanly. What do you do instead of `make install` on each server?
check.answer: Build once and make a **package** (rpm or deb, for example with `rpmbuild`, `fpm` or `checkinstall`) or install under `/opt/TOOL-VERSION` with a symlink, and distribute that artifact with your config management. Then install, upgrade and removal are tracked.

interview.q: What is the difference between rpm and dnf?
interview.a: rpm works on single package files and the local database. dnf adds repositories, dependency resolution and downloads, and calls rpm. See [the lesson](#/lesson/7/rpm-dnf).

interview.q: How do you find which package owns a file, on RPM and on Debian?
interview.a: `rpm -qf FILE` and `dpkg -S FILE`. See [the translation table](#/lesson/7/dpkg-apt).

interview.q: How can you check that installed files were not modified?
interview.a: `rpm -V PKG` (RPM) or `debsums` (Debian). It compares size, digest, mode and owner with the package database. See [rpm -V](#/lesson/7/rpm-dnf).

interview.q: What does `./configure && make && make install` do?
interview.a: configure probes the system and writes a Makefile, make compiles, make install copies files to the prefix. See [the lesson](#/lesson/7/build-from-source).

interview.q: Why is installing from source into /usr/local risky on a managed server?
interview.a: The package manager does not track the files, so upgrades, conflicts and removal become manual. Use a package or an /opt prefix.

interview.q: What does apt-get update do and what does it not do?
interview.a: It downloads repository package lists only. It installs and upgrades nothing.

glossary.def: An archive of files plus metadata and scripts, installed and tracked by a package manager.
An online catalog of packages with signed metadata.
Another package or library a package needs in order to work.
Low-level package tool and format of Red Hat family distributions.
Low-level package tool of Debian family distributions (.deb).
A file that lists build targets, prerequisites and recipes for make.
A staging root put in front of install paths so a build can be packaged without touching the system.
